definition: In this historical source, categories of thought are basic ways the mind organizes understanding, such as identity and difference. They are treated as logically linked abstractions that thinking uses to grasp reality, while in actual knowledge one or the other may be emphasized depending on the purpose of thought or action.

provenance.revision: 1901 New York Macmillan original; archive index checked 2026-10-18
provenance.scope: Source record Identitym; pinned source text

reasons: The definition characterizes “categories of thought” as “basic ways the mind organizes understanding,” but the packet does not describe categories of thought in terms of organizing understanding; it discusses identity and difference as metaphysical/logical conceptions and principles.

The packet supports that identity and difference are treated as logically correlative conceptions and that, for the thought using them, “one side or the other … subserves the interest of the thought or action,” but the definition’s broader claim that these are “abstractions that thinking uses to grasp reality” is not stated in the packet in that form.
